Elite Line Choice: Fastest, Smoothest or Most Repeatable?

  • Draft: ready for editorial review
  • Class 2
  • Release A

Performance outcome

The rider compares lines through a section by entry and exit speed, surface, traction, risk and what comes next, and chooses deliberately between the fastest, the smoothest and the most repeatable.

Who it’s for

Racers and fast riders who ride a section the same way every time, or who pick the line that looks fastest without knowing whether it is.

Before this lesson

  • Visual Focus and Reading the Trail.
  • Advanced Body Position.

Why it matters

The shortest line isn’t always the fastest, and the fastest line isn’t always the smoothest or safest. A line that is fast once but goes wrong one time in three may lose a race.

Technical model

Source check: d04 (video only: not yet watched), d05 (could not be opened). The reviewer must confirm this section against the original.

Speed, smoothness and agility

Lines can be chosen for outright speed, for smoothness (less energy lost, less fatigue) or for agility (setting up the next feature). Good riders know which they are choosing and why.

Look at the whole section

A line is judged by its exit and by what it sets up downstream, not just by how it feels in the middle.

Conditions change the answer

The fastest line on dry ground may be poor when wet or blown out. Line choice is revisited as conditions change through a race weekend.

Line choice versus confidence

A rider may avoid a faster line because of confidence rather than speed. Tracking these separately helps the coach see which one is limiting.

Physics & maths

Comparing lines with data

Two lines can be compared like an experiment: time each over the same section, several times, and compare the average and the spread, not just the best run. A line with a slightly slower average but a much smaller spread can be the better race choice.

A good Mathlete visual: two dot plots of segment times for line A and line B, with means and ranges.

Common errors

What you seePossible causesCorrection
Always riding the same line regardless of conditions.Habit; not re-walking or re-checking the section.Coach to supply
Choosing the line that looks fastest, then losing time at its exit.Judging the middle of the section rather than the exit.Coach to supply
A fast line that goes wrong often.Choosing speed over repeatability; line beyond current skill.Coach to supply

Practice design

Setting
A known section with two or more realistic lines, selected by the coach as suitable for the rider.
Focus
Ride each line several times; record times and the rider’s confidence separately.
Feedback
Annotated line map, segment times and side video of each line.

Stop when

  • A line feels beyond the rider’s current skill.
  • Conditions change.
  • Fatigue.

Video analysis

What the rider and coach look for in footage:

  • Entry and exit speed for each line.
  • Spread of times (consistency), not just the best.
  • Errors or corrections per run on each line.
  • Rider confidence rating (self-reported, kept separate from time).

Ready to move on

  • The rider can justify a line choice for a known section with timing, video and conditions, and the coach agrees with the reasoning.

Educational checkpoints, not safety certificates.

Safety

Class 2: advanced riding skills. Needs the stated prerequisites, a controlled progression, suitable terrain and coaching guidance.

Practice only on terrain your coach has chosen, within your current skill, with the right protective equipment. Completing a lesson isn’t a safety certificate and doesn’t mean a rider is ready to try anything.
